blocks.text: Dear Ms. Gonzalez:

This letter sets down the terms on which our firm will advise {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}} on its channel strategy, and it becomes our agreement at the moment you countersign the enclosed copy and return it to me. I have written it at some length, and in plainer language than a contract of this kind usually runs to, because an engagement proceeds more surely when the firm and the client have read the same account of it before any work is done, and because the hour spent settling expectations at the outset is repaid many times over across the months that follow. I would ask you to read what follows against your own understanding of the assignment, and to tell me of any point on which the two diverge before you sign, so that we begin from a description we both recognize rather than from two that only resemble one another.
What We Have Agreed to Examine

The assignment is a review of the routes through which {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}} takes its products to market, and its object is a channel strategy the company can defend on the economics rather than on habit. We will begin by setting down how the current channels actually perform, tracing the volume, the margin, and the cost to serve through each of them, so that the picture we work from is the one your operators would recognize and not the one the reporting has settled into over the years. From that base we will develop and weigh options for the channel mix, describing for each the operational and financial consequences we can stand behind, including those a preferred option would ask the company to accept. We will set the trade-offs out plainly rather than present a single recommendation as though it carried no cost, and we will keep the analysis close enough to the people who run the channels that the strategy we hand over is one your own team can act on after we have gone.

It is worth being equally clear about the boundary of the work. This is a channel strategy grounded in the current economics, not a pricing study, a systems selection, or a program to carry any recommendation into effect; and while we will lay out what a chosen direction asks of the organization, its execution will remain yours to lead unless we later agree, in writing, to a separate engagement covering that work. Should the scope of the assignment alter materially once we are underway, whether at your request or by what the analysis brings to light, we will describe the change and settle its terms with you before we act on it, so that nothing is added to the work without your assent.
Who Will Carry the Work

You will work with a small and constant team. Deborah Jimenez, our engagement manager, will hold the day-to-day conduct of the work and the cadence of our working sessions and reports, and she is the person to whom you should bring any question of pace or emphasis as the engagement proceeds. Joseph Reed will lead the quantitative side, the assembly and reconciliation of the channel economics on which every later recommendation will rest, and he will be answerable for seeing that the numbers we put in front of you tie and can withstand a hard question. I will keep the relationship at the level of the firm and remain accountable to you for what we deliver, so that the people whose names stand on our analysis are the people who have done it.
Our Fee and How We Will Bill It

Our fee for this engagement is a fixed {{fact:f:E-2020-002.fee}}, which covers the work described above together with the ordinary meetings, correspondence, and interim materials that accompany it. It does not extend to work we might later agree to add, such as carrying a chosen channel strategy into operation, which we would scope and price separately before beginning. We will invoice against the fee at regular intervals as the work proceeds, and each invoice falls due within thirty days of its date.
Duration and Bringing the Engagement to an End

The engagement will commence on {{fact:f:E-2020-002.start}} and is scoped to run for approximately five months, that being the period over which we have planned the analysis and the option work, though I will tell you early if the assignment proves to need more time or less. Either party may bring it to an end on reasonable written notice to the other. Should you choose to end it, you will owe the fee earned to the date of termination together with any costs properly incurred to that point, and nothing further; should we do so, which we would undertake only for a reason our professional standards require, we will refund any part of the fee that relates to work not yet performed and will help hand the assignment over in good order.
Confidential Information

We will treat the information you place in our hands, together with the fact and the substance of this engagement, as confidential, and we will use what you disclose to us solely for the work you have retained us to perform. We ask the same of {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}} in respect of the methods, analyses, and materials we bring to the assignment. These obligations will outlast the completion or termination of the engagement, and neither party will disclose the other's confidential information except where the law or a proper authority compels it, and then only so far as compelled and, where practicable, on notice to the other.
The Limits of Our Responsibility

We will perform this engagement with the care and skill our profession expects, and our advice will represent our considered judgment on the information available to us. We do not, however, warrant a particular commercial result, since the outcome of a change in channel strategy turns in large part on decisions and actions that rest with your organization rather than with ours. Our aggregate liability arising out of or in connection with this engagement will be limited to the amount of the fee actually paid to us under it, save where the law does not permit such a limit, and neither party will be liable to the other for indirect or consequential loss.
Governing Law and the Whole of Our Agreement

This letter constitutes the entire agreement between us in respect of this engagement and supersedes any prior discussion or understanding, and it may be varied only by a writing signed by both parties. It will be governed by, and construed in accordance with, the law of the state in which our firm maintains its principal office, and each of us submits to the jurisdiction of the courts of that state in respect of any dispute arising under it.

If the terms set out above reflect our understanding, I would ask you to sign and date the enclosed copy of this letter and return it to me, upon which we will confirm the commencement and begin the work. If any part of it warrants discussion first, tell me and I will make the time this week to talk it through before you sign.
Sincerely,

This engagement is about how {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}} reaches its market. We are here to sort out which channels earn their place and which do not. Our sponsor on the client side is Julie Gonzalez, their Director of Operations, and she has been clear that she wants a strategy her own team can run, not one that only reads well in a deck. That standard should shape what we look at first. I want to set out how I see the work dividing before we begin.

A word on how we will work with the client. Julie Gonzalez and her team hold the data and the day-to-day knowledge of the channels, so the pace of the analysis depends on a steady, light flow of requests rather than one large ask up front. We will keep each request small and specific, and we will tell them plainly when something we asked for turns out not to matter. The more we behave like part of their week and less like an audit, the faster the good data comes back.
How the work divides

items: Map the channels as they run today. Every route to market, the volume through each, and who owns it on the client side.

Build the channel economics. Margin and cost to serve, route by route, reconciled to the ledger so a later recommendation rests on a measured number and not a guess. I will own this piece and open the data requests in the first week.
Shape the options. Two or three candidate channel mixes, each tested against today for what it earns and what it asks the organization to change.
Plan the handover. Once a direction is set, lay out the steps and the owners so the client's team can carry it forward without us in the room.

blocks.text: These are not four separate projects. The map feeds the economics. The economics discipline the options. The handover only makes sense once a direction is settled. I put them in this order on purpose. The temptation on work like this is to jump to the options before the current picture is solid, and options built on a shaky base tend to come apart the first time they meet a number from the floor. We will hold the order even when the client would like to see options sooner.

One habit I want us to hold from the first day. Every number we put in front of the client should tie to something in their ledger, and we should be able to say where it came from. When we cannot, we say so, and we mark the figure as provisional until it firms up. That is how the economics stay trustworthy as the options take shape.
First moves

Work begins on {{fact:f:E-2020-002.start}}. I will get the first data request to Julie Gonzalez's team by the end of the first week, kept deliberately short so we are not waiting on a long list before we can start. The early request is only the channel volumes and the cost lines behind them, which is enough to stand the economics up and to show the client what a small, specific ask looks like.

A couple of things on our side. Deborah Jimenez will keep the cadence of our working sessions and the client status reports, so the rhythm is set from the outset. I would also like the two of us to walk through the approach together before we sit down with the client, so we arrive with one account of it and not two.

I will circulate a short, dated schedule ahead of the first client session, with our internal checkpoints marked on it. If either of us sees a conflict in the opening weeks, tell me and we will work around it before the client dates are fixed.
The first step is the data request. I will draft it this week and send it to Deborah Jimenez for a look before it goes to the client.
Hello Julie,

Thank you for the channel volumes your team sent through last week. We have most of what we need to start the economics for {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}}, and the early read is that the split by route looks much as your operators described it. One gap is worth flagging while it is small. The direct and distributor volumes for the last two quarters arrive under a single line, so we cannot yet see the cost to serve for each of them on its own.

Two things would help from here. If someone on your side can separate those two lines, or simply point me to where the underlying detail sits, we can keep the cost picture moving without waiting on a full re-cut. And I would still like thirty minutes each with the two channel managers you flagged, so the economics are tested against how the channels really run.

On scheduling, Deborah Jimenez will hold times open late next week and send you a short list to choose from. Send whatever is easiest straight to me, Joseph Reed, and I will get it into the model the same day. I know this lands in a full week for you, Julie Gonzalez, and I have kept the asks as small as the work allows.
Best regards
Working Session -- Channel Strategy for {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}}

The session settled one point that shapes the next two weeks: we will close the channel economics and move to option design, once the distributor cost-to-serve figures are confirmed. The channel map holds. The economics are all but complete. These minutes record who attended, what we covered, and who owns each next step.
Present
Where the economics stand

Joseph Reed walked through the channel economics. Margin and cost to serve are now built for every route to market. The picture lines up with the channel map from the earlier weeks, with the usual small gaps between the documented flow and the real one. One figure is still soft. The cost to serve for the distributor channel rests on an allocation the client's finance team has not yet confirmed. Until that lands, the distributor margin stays provisional. Nothing else in the economics is open.

The early reading is worth recording. At least one route carries more cost to serve than its share of volume would suggest. That is not a finding yet, only a signal, and the option work is where it gets tested. We agreed not to draw conclusions from it before the allocation is confirmed.
Data still open

One item is outstanding on the client side. The distributor cost-to-serve allocation sits with the finance team and has not come back. Joseph Reed has told them exactly what he needs to split it. The request is small and specific, and it should not take a full re-post to answer.
The standard the strategy has to meet

Julie Gonzalez restated the test for the work. Her managers have to be able to run the new channel mix after we leave. She has seen strategies that read well and stalled in operation. We agreed to describe each option in terms of what it asks her team to do differently. An elegant mix her people cannot run does not count as a candidate.
Moving to options

The plan from here is two or three candidate channel mixes. Each is tested against today for what it earns and what it changes. We agreed not to show options before the economics are firm. Julie Gonzalez asked whether confirming the distributor figures puts the finish at risk. It does not, provided the finance team returns the allocation inside the week. The option work is scoped to absorb the short hold without moving the end of the engagement.
Action items

rows: Have the finance team confirm the distributor cost-to-serve allocation, or point Joseph Reed to the underlying detail
Close the channel economics once the allocation is confirmed and lock the base for option design
Confirm the option-review date with the client and circulate the agenda

blocks.text: The next step is the allocation. Once finance returns it, Joseph Reed closes the economics and option design begins. Nothing downstream moves until that figure is confirmed.
Status Report -- Channel Strategy for {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}}

This is our midpoint update on the channel strategy work for {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}}. Joseph Reed prepared it and Deborah Jimenez has reviewed it. It covers where we stand, what we have done since the last report, what comes next, and the few things we are watching.
Where we stand

The work is on plan at the midpoint. The channel map is settled and the economics are nearly closed. We have moved from understanding the current channels to shaping the options that will follow them. There is no change to scope, fee, or timeline requested in this report.

Effort and cost to date sit within the fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2020-002.fee}}. We have spent roughly what we expected to at this stage, weighted toward the analysis, and we see nothing in the remaining work that would push us past it. Your team has kept pace with our requests, which is a large part of why we are on plan. When the flow of data is steady, the analysis does not stall, and that has been the pattern so far.
What we have done since the last report

We finished the channel map. Every route {{fact:f:E-2020-002.client}} uses to reach its market is now traced, with the volume and the internal owner recorded for each. Where the documented flow and the real one differed, we took the real one, which is the point of doing the map at all. The map is the base everything else is built on, so we held it open until your operators agreed it matched what they see.

We built the channel economics. Margin and cost to serve are now assembled route by route and reconciled to the ledger, so the recommendations to come will rest on measured numbers rather than estimates. Reconciling to the ledger took longer than a rough estimate would have, and it is worth it, because a number that ties can survive a hard question in a way an estimate cannot. The early reading is that at least one route carries more cost to serve than its share of volume would suggest, which is exactly the kind of thing the option work has to weigh.

We closed most of the open data. Your team turned the channel volumes around quickly. Only one figure, the distributor cost-to-serve allocation, is still with finance, and until it lands that part of the picture stays provisional. We have kept the request for it small and specific so it is easy to answer.
What comes next

The next phase is option design. We will shape two or three candidate channel mixes and test each against today for what it earns and what it asks the organization to change. We will describe every option in terms your managers can act on, because a mix the team cannot run is not a real option.

Each option will carry its own economics, so a choice between them is a choice you can make on the numbers and not on impression. We will also be plain about what each one asks of the organization to stand up, since the cost of a change is part of its price and belongs in the comparison.

We expect to bring the options and their trade-offs to you before any direction is fixed. Our aim is a clear, honest set of choices, each with its costs shown, so that the decision is yours to make on the merits. We will lay the options side by side and walk your team through them in a working session before anything is settled.
What we are watching

Two things could affect pace, and neither threatens the result. The first is the distributor allocation still with finance; until it lands, the distributor margin stays provisional, and we have asked for it inside the week. The second is calendar time with the two channel managers, which we need to test the options against how the channels actually run.

Deborah Jimenez is holding those sessions open and will confirm them as soon as your side can. Neither item is on a critical path yet, and we will flag it plainly here the moment either one starts to bite.

The one thing that moves everything forward is the distributor allocation. Once finance returns it, we close the economics and start the option design, and we will send you the option-review date the same week.
